stories.title: Nvidia Without Jensen Huang: A Power Vacuum at the AI Apex
stories.story:
Four days after Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation, Nvidia — the company whose chips are the central nervous system of the global AI build-out — arrives at its most consequential week without its founder at the helm. The scandal's mechanics matter as much as its drama. Huang had been conducting an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national who served as an executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company that had grown into a major Nvidia chip buyer, reportedly poised to spend $2 billion more on Nvidia AI technology. U.S. Commerce Department investigators had been examining whether Megaspeed was helping Chinese firms circumvent American export controls — and whether the relationship between the two Huangs was the channel through which 240,000 banned chips reached China.

The board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO, president, and director on November 11. Colette Kress, the CFO, is now interim chief. Today, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly urged the board to appoint an external CEO, calling for a "dramatic shake-up," while simultaneously demanding answers within ten days about whether Nvidia knowingly facilitated restricted chip sales through Megaspeed. Meanwhile, a petition to reinstate Huang has gathered over 106,000 signatures, backed by Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

The timing is brutal. Nvidia reports Q3 earnings on Tuesday under a CFO-turned-interim-CEO. Anthropic prices what may be the largest AI IPO ever on Wednesday. Markets are already rattled — Asian chip indices fell more than 6% intraday today. The deeper implication is structural: for years, Nvidia's strategic coherence — its near-monopoly on AI training hardware, its software moat — was inseparable from Huang's judgment. Export controls exist precisely to prevent adversaries from acquiring the hardware. The question now is whether the control architecture failed not through policy, but through proximity.
stories.hook: The chip export regime was built to stop states — it may have been undone by a dinner reservation in Singapore.
stories.source: CBS News, Wikipedia (Jensen Huang spying scandal), Newsquawk, Wall Street Journal via Rallies.ai

stories.title: OpenAI Gives Its AI Agents a Wallet and a Spending Account
stories.story:
For decades, the missing link in e-commerce automation was not intelligence — it was permission. A system could know what you wanted, find the best price, and fill the cart, but it couldn't pull the trigger without your card number sitting somewhere it shouldn't. OpenAI just solved the permission problem.

On November 13, ChatGPT Wallet went live for Pro subscribers in the United States. The mechanic is precise: you register a card once, and when OpenAI's always-on "dots" agent wants to complete a purchase, it triggers a biometric check — Face ID or fingerprint — on your device. Only after that tap does the payment network generate a single-use substitute credential: a scoped card number, security code, and expiration date that the merchant processes and then discards. The agent itself never sees your real card. Neither does the retailer.

The partners — American Express, Mastercard, and Visa — are not incidental. American Express is calling this its first "Agentic Commerce Experiences" integration. The card networks have spent years building tokenization rails for Apple Pay and Google Pay; ChatGPT Wallet is the first deployment of that infrastructure for a third-party AI agent operating semi-autonomously.

The business logic OpenAI is building toward is more ambitious than the launch version. The company has indicated it expects users to eventually grant agents standing authorization — bounded by spending limits, merchant categories, or time windows — so that routine purchases clear without any human tap at all. OpenAI has also said it is not taking a cut of transactions at launch, which means the current product is a trust-building exercise, not a revenue line.

What changes is the competitive map of commerce. If AI agents with payment authority become normalized, the question is no longer which search engine you use — it is which agent your household trusts to shop. That is a stickier relationship than any browser default.
stories.hook: The real question isn't whether AI can shop for you — it's which AI you trust enough to let it.

stories.title: Anthropic's $90 Billion IPO Is Two Days Away
stories.story:
On Wednesday, Anthropic will attempt to price the largest technology IPO in history. The five-year-old maker of the Claude AI models has set a range of $70 to $78 per share for 825 million Class A shares, targeting up to $64.4 billion in public proceeds. A separate $26 billion private placement with Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC brings the total raise to as much as $90.4 billion — roughly five times the size of the Google IPO in 2004.

The structural details are unusual and revealing. The book is reportedly six times oversubscribed, yet bankers deliberately set the range below initial expectations, a tactic borrowed from the playbook of deals that want room to run on debut rather than top-tick the market. The seven strategic buyers in the private placement hold stock with no lockup, meaning the first day of trading will also be the first day any of them can sell. That is not standard, and it places an enormous amount of trust — or pressure — on the opening price.

The deeper story is what the deal reveals about where the AI economy now sits. Anthropic is not a chip company or a cloud platform; it is a pure-play model developer that loses money at scale. Its revenues are real and growing fast, but its compute commitments run to tens of billions and its S-1 describes losses rather than profits. What investors are buying is not earnings — it is a position in the AI layer that could be worth everything or, as one notable bear put it last week, the peak of the trade.

The timing adds irony. Anthropic prices two days after Nvidia — the company whose chips Anthropic depends on — reports its first earnings under an interim CEO. The entire AI financial complex, from semiconductor to model to investor wallet, converges in a single week.
stories.hook: The first pure-play AI company to go public is raising more money than any company in history — while still posting losses.

stories.title: Washington Picks Its AI Winners — Before the Market Does
stories.story:
The Trump administration is preparing to formally designate more than two dozen American technology companies — including Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic — as artificial intelligence "national champions," according to a Wall Street Journal report published Sunday night. The label, initially floated roughly a year ago as part of the administration's broader technology strategy, had never come with a public list until now.

The concrete mechanics matter more than the branding. According to the WSJ, designated firms would receive expedited export licence approvals for chips and other advanced technology, direct government support for overseas operations, and access to federal financing. In effect, Washington would be bundling the state's commercial and diplomatic weight behind a chosen cohort of private firms — much as France once shielded its nuclear and aerospace industries, or South Korea cultivated its chaebols.

The timing is charged. The announcement lands as Nvidia is in leadership freefall, its share price down sharply since Jensen Huang's resignation, with Treasury Secretary Bessent publicly demanding an external CEO and an export-control compliance review. Bestowing "national champion" status on a company whose former chief is alleged to have had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy creates an immediate tension: the designation is designed to accelerate overseas expansion of exactly the chip technology that Washington's other hand is trying to restrict.

The deeper implication is industrial-policy drift. For decades the U.S. resisted picking corporate winners on principle, leaving that to markets. If the national champions list survives legal and congressional scrutiny, it sets a precedent — companies outside the circle gain a structural disadvantage in winning foreign government contracts, while those inside become, in a meaningful sense, instruments of foreign policy. The line between private enterprise and state enterprise quietly moves.
stories.hook: America spent forty years lecturing the world against industrial policy — and then quietly decided it wanted one.
stories.source: The Wall Street Journal / Reuters, November 15–16, 2026

stories.title: The Fed Reverses Course: A December Rate Hike Is Now Expected
stories.story:
For most of 2026, markets had been braced for interest-rate cuts. What arrived instead was something nobody on Wall Street had penciled in at the start of the year: a Federal Reserve preparing to raise rates in December, potentially followed by more hikes in January.

The pivot traces back to a single data point. A hotter-than-expected October CPI print, released November 10, showed headline inflation rising 0.4% month-on-month, with core CPI — the Fed's preferred signal — still running at 0.3%. Producer prices added to the picture, with core PPI advancing at a 4.9% annual rate. The labor market offered no cover either; continuing claims fell to 1.69 million, suggesting employers aren't flinching.

The bond market moved immediately. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed roughly 30 basis points in five sessions, crossing 5.15% — its largest weekly jump since April 2025. That repricing rippled outward: 10-year yields rose in Germany, the UK, and Japan in sympathy. A stronger dollar pressured non-US equities even as American stocks, paradoxically, finished the week up 2.5%.

Fed Governor Waller had already warned that a 50 basis-point hike in December could be warranted if core CPI came in at 0.3% or above. It did. Deutsche Bank now forecasts three consecutive hikes. Prediction markets put December at roughly 75–80% odds. Chair Kevin Warsh held at 3.75–4.00% in October — but two governors dissented in favor of hiking even then.

The deeper irony is structural. The very AI capital expenditure boom driving equity valuations is itself inflationary: power demand, construction, and specialized labor don't come cheap. The Fed may be tightening precisely because the technology story is succeeding too fast.
stories.hook: The Fed spent a year cutting rates to stimulate the economy — and now the economy it stimulated is forcing it to raise them again.
stories.source: Newsquawk / The Investing Group / Rio Times, November 16, 2026
